p: I don't have the percentage with me right now.

We can get back to you on that.
Please do, Chair, because this is important.
Yes, we can follow up with that.
They say that, but we need to see it also.
Thank you, THank you for your questions. Council Member Wong.

Uhm, yes, um, thank you, Chair. Um, my office deals with a lot of seniors, seniors that either don't know how to scan documents or upload to, uh, like an application like Fair Fares NYC. Um, or they simply, uh, don't know how to, uh, apply because it's such a complicated process. I didn't count the number of pages, but it is just not easy, uh, for anybody that never scanned documents before in their life, or, or the, the only thing they know to do with the cell phone is to make phone calls. You know, they, they just don't know how to upload documents to a portal. Okay, um, so what I, uh, what I want to know is that, do you have, like, a paper option where someone can actually do it the old-fashioned way, make copies of the documents and send it in? Because I think a lot of seniors, at least in my district, uh, would, would do— would be able to do that, but they would have a very difficult time navigating your website and apply online to the Fair Share NYC. Can you— can you talk about that? Would a paper option be possible?

Thank you, Council Member, for their question. Um, Fair Fares eligibility is up to 64. The senior population is, um, uh, sorry, it’s covered by the MTA. So that question should be directed to the MTA. As you said, they will be here later.

But, but to, you know, just to add to that, I just wanted to, you know, reiterate that yes, we understand that, you know, there might be, um, uh, digital barriers to access. That's why we have the 5 in-person centers. And it's also really why we lean heavily into our community, uh, um, our CBO partners, because they can actually, you know, help in that process in, uh, making sure that they're, uh, walking people through the application process.

Yeah and I also want to say that, uh, due to language barriers, they may have difficulty in reading, the, uh, or understanding the application, uh, in the, in the English form. So you gotta make sure that it is available in several languages. I think that is also another barrier that you have to overcome. I mean, 550,000 people eligible but did not enroll. That's 60% of the

people out there that we can service but either don't bother because it's complicated or just, they just don't know about it. Oh, I'll say, Council Member, if there are, um, constituencies that you feel, um, that need, you know, more, uh, accessibility, we're happy to work with you and anyone else up here, um, you know, to make sure that we're paying attention.

Yeah, perhaps you can send us a portal and one of my staff will upload all the applications in one batch rather than making them apply individually, you know. That's something we can definitely work on.
Yeah, we can absolutely work with your office, Council Member, on a pop-up or any way to support.
Thank you. Council Member Morano.

Thank you, Chair. Uh, thank you, Ms. Chew for your testimony and everybody else. Um, your testimony says DSS already auto-enrolls people into HEAP when they're receiving SNAP or cash assistance and that those cases are fast-tracked in roughly 2 to 3 minutes. So if the

infrastructure already exists, why has Fair Fares remained a separate bureaucratic process for so long?

Uh, thank you, Council Member Morano, for your, uh, for your question. Um, so for HEAP, we— in order to, um, have, you know sort of reciprocity with HEAP, we had to work very closely with our state oversight agencies, um, OTDA, because of the, you know, confidential nature of the information in connection with people's public benefits applications for, uh, cash assistance and SNAP, um, in order to be able to, um, you know, um, have the autopay file through

You spent a great deal of time in your testimony talking about privacy concerns, and I appreciate the privacy concerns you raised. But millions of New Yorkers already give the city extremely sensitive information for taxes, SNAP, Medicaid, housing assistance, and public schools. So where exactly is the line? At what point does privacy become an excuse for maintaining unnecessary bureaucracy?

Right. Thank you. Oh, thank you for your question. So, you know, we, we very much believe in, in people's right to free agency and to

privacy in their personal information. So when they're applying for a public benefit, um, you know, we have to protect that information, whether it is about their domestic violence status or health information or, um, income information. All of that is highly protected information governed by, you know, state and federal, uh, laws and regulations that that there are boundaries, even within our own social services agency, that we cannot just, you know, share that information without, um, you know, the, the client's express consent and permission, um, and also in consultation with our oversight agencies. And, uh, Chair, if you'll permit me, one final question on the replacement—
Sure thing.

Card bill. Um, you— I'm proud to be a sponsor of the Replacement Card bill, and your testimony says participants can already switch the discount to a debit card, credit card, phone, or OMNY Card but if we're being realistic, a lot of low-income New Yorkers don't always have stable banking access, smartphones, or reliable technology. Isn't that exactly why physical replacement cards still matter?

Um, thank you, Council Member, for your questions. Um, so yes, when someone is eligible for, uh, the Fair Fares, uh, program, they can elect to have, um, us mail the physical OMNY Card. Um, they can also elect to use, um, you know, their smart phone or link it to a credit card or debit card or their own OMNY Card. Um, and so, you know, there's multiple options there, including, like, you said, the physical card. Um, and for, um, you know, HRA, um, if someone needs a replacement card for their lost OMNY Card, again, even though there's innovations now where there's multiple, um, facet— you know, ways to, to access the, the Fair Fares Discount, you know, through all those different, um, you know, types of, uh, options, uh, we can also mail out, you know, a replacement OMNY Card if that's the primary, um, way that people are using, um, participation in the program.
Thank you.

Thank you so much. HRA administers Fair Fares applications through Access HRA and through 5 Fair Fares offices. Enrollment lasts for 1 year and may be renewed as long as the

participant continues to meet eligibility requirements. Applicants are notified by mail after review, which may take up to 30 days. How long does it currently take on average for an eligible applicant to be approved for Fair Fares?
Um, thank you, Chair Hudson, for your question. Um, it takes approximately 4 days.
Yes.
How many Fair Fares applications are currently pending?
Uh, approximately 1,500 are currently pending, and none of them are over 30 days pending.
Okay and— okay, so there are none pending for more than 30 days currently?
Yes.

Okay and, um, what are some of the most common reasons applications are denied, delayed, or abandoned? We heard from, um, one person this morning at the rally, you know, that she was $1,000 over the eligibility requirement. So I'm curious to know, is it, is it income? Is it residency?

Thank you for the question, Council Chair. Generally, it is for income, um, or sometimes it's incorrect documents, um, and income eligibility, of course, is the major reason why people are, uh, denied.
And, um, what's the process if, if somebody— if, if the reason is for, um, the paperwork, right, that you just mentioned. What's the process for helping folks to correct that paperwork?
There is a notice that goes out, um, to the individual that allows them to know what the issue was, and they have that ability to correct it, uh, within, uh, 30 days.
And how do they receive that notice?
In the mail.
In the mail, okay. Um, how many Fair Fares applications were submitted in fiscal year 2025 and fiscal year 2026 to date?
Uh, yes 231,270 applications, uh, were initiated in fiscal year '25. Um, 118,009 were approved. Uh, 51,018 were denied. 160—
Wait, I'm sorry. You're still talking about fiscal year '25?
Yes.
Okay, so 118,009 were approved.
Yes.
And how many did you say were 50—
Uh, 51,018, 5-1-0-1-8, were denied. Um, 168 were canceled.
Um, canceled by HRA?
No, by the client.
Oh, by the client, okay.
Um, and 62,071 were incomplete. That was for, um, fiscal year '25. I can go over it again, or we can send it after.
No, that's perfect. I have the numbers. Do you have for, um, to date on fiscal year '26?
Yes.
The same stats.

191,224 applications have been initiated so far in fiscal year '26. 99,083 have

been approved. 38,606 were denied. 99 were canceled and 45,502 have been incomplete.

And so— for the incomplete— um, the incomplete applications, those are the ones where people are notified by mail that their applications were incomplete and have an opportunity to then resubmit paperwork or?

No, the denials are the ones that receive a notification in the mail. Incomplete they have emails and text messages that say hey your application is incomplete, you need to upload documents and, for whatever reason, they're not uploading the document.
And then, um, maybe you have this for fiscal year 2025, but I'm just curious to know, of those incomplete applications, how many are then within a certain amount of time or ultimately, um, approved?
We don't have that statistic. What happens is that incomplete application expires after 10 days, and so they would have to restart the application.
So once they've been notified of incompletion, then they have 10 days to correct, and after that they'd have to reapply?
Start a new application, yes.

Okay. I think that is just another example of where we can create an efficiency and maybe, you know, not limit ourselves or limit clients or potential, um, enrollees to just 10 days to complete an application and maybe even extend it to 30 days. I personally don't understand why there would need to be a time limit anyway. But if there must be, maybe 30 days so that people can have the time to resubmit rather than just 10 days. It feels a little tight. Um, but thank you for those numbers. It's— we appreciate the, the, the data. Um, are applicants able to submit all necessary documents through Access HRA and the mobile app? Or there's some that have to be submitted another way?
Uh, yes. Um, applicants are able to submit all necessary documents through Access HRA, uh, the mobile app, and the vast majority of applicants do apply and renew online.
They do-
Apply and also renew, um, online.
Okay. And what percentage of Fair Fares participants successfully renew their enrollment each year?
Um, over the past 2 years, approximately 50% of clients, um, have not, uh, renewed.
So 50% have renewed and 50% have not renewed?
Yes.
And— is— so does that mean 50% of the people lose their benefits because they don't complete the renewal on time?
Uh, well, roughly 50%, um, you know, —fall out of the program, um, also—
Fall out of the program, meaning they're no longer eligible?

Uh, well, they were not renewed for the program, so they would have fallen out of the program, but about 19% of the clients who dropped off because of failing to renew do return to the program within 120 days.

Okay, so, you know, I think this is— another opportunity for efficiency where if

we know people are eligible, I mean, why are we even asking them to renew? If they're eligible, they're eligible and shouldn't we just automatically renew their applications?
So I think this is, you know, one of the things that's kind of core to, uh, why we want to take a look at what's being proposed here.
Yes.
Is, um, you know, the threshold of consent, um, you know, is still there for, you know, um, uh, for clients that for some reason might not necessarily wanna be in the program.
Right.

I think we could certainly look at, um, maybe ways we can, um, increase, you know, interaction and make sure that we're, that, um, we're creating maybe another layer of, uh, interaction to, uh, make sure people don't fall off, but, uh—

Yeah, I mean, I think the consent I'm with you on, and— but I think there's— it's one thing to ask people if they consent to being re-enrolled in the program. It's another thing to

ask people to re-enroll in the program. And if half of the people who are enrolled in the program are then falling out of the program simply because they're— they have to re-enroll, or renew, I think we're failing.
So we're happy to continue, uh, taking a look at that and figuring out what efficiencies.

Okay and it also, it just seems like, you know, hamster in the wheel, like we, we still haven't, we still haven't gotten to 100%, um, enrollment or whatever for every eligible New Yorker we know exists. And then we're at— we're losing people because we're asking them to renew, and then we're trying to get them back, and then it's just like this continuous cycle, and we're still not getting to as many people enrolled in the program as possible. And so, you know, I would love to, you know, be a partner to you all in thinking about how do we create efficiencies in the application process specifically to, um, to guarantee more— greater enrollment, but, you know, easier access throughout the process.
Absolutely. We're happy to continue that conversation.
Um, do you send renewal reminders?

Um, yes, uh, we send out letters, text messages, and emails to remind enrollees to renew. Um, we send out a letter 90 days, um, to the renewal period. Um and then another 30 days prior, and also text messages 3 days prior to the renewal expiration.
And what about the emails?
Emails are sent 30 days before the expiration of renewal.

Okay. So letters 90 days and then 30 days, text message 3 days, and emails 30 days. Okay. Um, I wanted to ask a question. Um, in, in your, uh, testimony, Chief Chew, you mentioned that 2/3 of Fairfax clients, you enroll via the, ah, fast-track program. And I'm just, I'm curious to know, the difference between those who are currently in— if you have this information— of the eligible New Yorkers, how many are already in the HRA system versus not? And if you have that or would know that information.

I guess what I'm trying to get at is if two-thirds of the clients are using this system, perhaps the remaining third could be or would be using the system. And so I'm wondering if it's because either they're not in the— they may not be receiving cash assistance or SNAP, um, or if they are, you know, how can we get to that last third of people?
Yeah, let us dig into that and we'll get back to you.

Okay, sure. Um, okay, so the Council needs reliable data to evaluate whether Fair Fares is reaching eligible New Yorkers, reducing transportation hardship, and operating efficiently. We'd like to get a better understanding of the current enrollees of Fair Fares and forgive me if some of these questions are redundant, and if we've already gone over them, then we can skip them. Um, do you have the breakout by borough for active enrollees?

Uh, yes. So enrollment by borough as of, um, March 31st, 2026, on the enrollment in each borough is for the Bronx, 99,570. For Brooklyn, 125,891, for Manhattan, 65,296, for Queens, 77,451,

for Staten Island, 11,702. Um, you may not— have this, but, uh, do you have eligibility based on borough? So of the total number of eligible New Yorkers, do you know the borough breakdown?
We don't have that. We'll have to dig into seeing whether that's something that—

Okay, because I— what would like to figure out is the percentage of people in each borough, and if perhaps we need to work a little bit more with certain CBOs, or think about the Fair Fare offices. Um, I would guess, because the 5 poorest Council districts are all in the Bronx, one, uh, straddles the Bronx and Manhattan, Council Member Encarnacion's district, and— Bronx enrollment is lower than Brooklyn enrollment. And so my guess is that there are more people who are eligible and not enrolled in the Bronx perhaps than in other boroughs. And so just trying to figure out the delta there between how many, how many eligible New Yorkers are in the Bronx versus how many are actually enrolled and proportionately allocating our resources and investments into each of the boroughs based on that?
Yeah, no, I think that's a good question. Um, I mean, we would only know the folks that are already within our HRA world, but that's something we can, you know, dig into.

Okay, yeah, I mean, even knowing how many are in the Bronx that are eligible versus that are enrolled, you know, and for each borough would still be helpful, I think, if not the total universe. What's the percent of unduplicated Fair Fares eligible households in the current HRA benefits universe that are not enrolled?

We don't have the percent of unduplicated Fair Fares eligible households that are not enrolled. However, I think we said it, ah, a little earlier, but 67.4% of Fast Track eligible, ah, Clients, those are— those enrolled in SNAP in— or cash assistance are, um, unenrolled in the Fair Fares program.
Okay, thank you, helpful and, um, how often is the total enrollment data updated on HRA's website?
Uh, it's updated monthly.
Monthly?
Yes.
Okay and—
Sorry, I'm so sorry, weekly. Thank you.
Weekly, even better. Um, does that number include currently enrolled and active users or something else?
Uh, current enrollees.
Current enrollees, okay. And how many HRA clients qualify for other transit subsidy programs and thus do not need Fair Fares?
Um, we don't have that information.
Okay. It would be good to get that if you—
Yeah, let us—
If you can look into it?
Let's see what we can pull together.
Okay, thank you. What's the average income and age for current active Fair Fare enrollees?

Um, we'll have to get back to you on that. Okay and you do not collect employment status, right? So you wouldn't be able to provide a

breakdown of the current active Fair Fares enrollees by employment status?
Uh, yes, Chair. We don't, uh, collect employment information for Fair Fares.
Okay and do you track Fair Fares usage after enrollment?
Um, yes, we do.
And do you have, uh, numbers on that, or how often are enrolled participants actually using the discount?
Sure, historically, um, usage has been around 50%. Um, since the expansion to OMNY, uh, program usage has risen, averaging now 56%, um, in fiscal year '26.
Okay and how do you collect feedback from participants about outreach efforts and the program itself?

Sure. So, um, you know, we, um, mentioned before that we have had a few, you know, surveys to check for, you know, client satisfactions. We also, um, you know, may receive calls through our one number system, um, to get feedback from, uh, Fair Fares participants.
Okay, thank you and how many Fair Fares related complaints has HRA received in fiscal year 2026 to date?
Um, we've received, uh, 826.
And what are the most common reasons for complaint?

Um, so during fiscal year 2026, this was the transition to OMNY, so many of those calls were related to, um, not having access to reload their Metro Card, um, and that vending machines were no longer available at their, um, stations. So we took those opportunities to transition those clients over into OMNY so that they had access to their discount.

Okay, thank you. I'd like to acknowledge that we've been joined by Council Members Stevens and Krishnan. Um, and then, what assessments have you undertaken related to the impact of Fair Fares? Are there plans to undertake any assessments in the future?

Um, we have conducted, um, various, you know, Fair Fare studies, um, and surveys, um, to get, um, feedback, and going forward

we do plan to continue this work, um, you know, and, um, you know, the focus of, of future assessments is, is under discussion.

Okay, thank you. Um, I just want to get into the legislation, and I think we're gonna move on to the MTA in a few. And actually, before I do that, I do want to ask— you have questions? Okay. I do want to ask a question um for Council Member Brooks-Powers, who had to leave. Um, 2 questions from her. Given the cost— given the high cost of living in New York City, how is the Administration evaluating the need to expand Fair Fares eligibility beyond current thresholds? And what data are you using to assess how many additional New Yorkers would benefit from an expansion to 200% of the federal poverty level and beyond?
So that is, you know, as with the other Council and advocate proposals still being reviewed right now. And so, um, you know, once we have more to share, we'll certainly share with this group.

Okay, and then she also wants to know, um, or she says thousands of eligible

New Yorkers are still not enrolled in Fair Fares. Can you walk us through where the biggest drop-offs are in the enrollment process and what concrete steps your agency is taking to ensure eligible individuals, particularly those already receiving public benefits, are automatically connected to this program?

Sure. So, um, you know, we, um, will continue to kind of review those proposals, um, you know, and, and examine and encourage, rather, um, eligible New Yorkers who qualify for Fair Fares to apply for Fair Fares and better understand kind of like, you know, and factoring in there's things out of our control such as, uh, commuter preferences or modes of transportation preferences also.

Okay, um, thank you. I'm going to turn it over to Council Member Sanchez, who has a couple questions. Then I'll come back with some questions specific to the legislation, and then we'll move on to the MTA. Thank you.

Thank you, thank you so much Chair, uh, and Chairs, and good morning. Um, you know, just echoing support for the legislation that is being considered today. Um, I represent the Northwest Bronx, Kingsbridge, Fordham, University

Heights, and I think, uh, as Chair Hudson pointed out when she was speaking about the 4 lowest-income districts being in the Bronx, I think probably no other Council Members understand, uh, as deeply as we do how difficult it is to reach low-income New Yorkers, right? Um, in my office, we served, like, 15,000 constituents in the first 4 years, and all of that was, like, people who walked into our office or, you know, we met them on the street or something like that. It's really tough to reach people. So I— my first question is, um, regarding the, you know, relatively low rates of folks who are enrolled, eligible folks that are enrolled, that 39.9%. In your estimation, where do you think we're losing folks in the pipeline? Is it awareness? Is it the application completion? Is it documentation requirements, recertification, approval delays? Where, where do you think the problem is?
